title: Consider your ways (Haggai 1:2–8)
hookLine: you eat but aren't full; you earn wages into a bag with holes

lines: PAYDAY, AND IT'S GONE BY FRIDAY.
A BAG WITH HOLES IN IT.
cards: Payday. The money lands, and by the end of the week, somehow, it's gone. Not on anything big.
Just leaking: groceries that didn't last, subscriptions you forgot, little fixes on things that keep breaking. Working hard and never quite getting ahead.
An old prophet named Haggai described exactly that, with an image anyone who's carried coins can picture: a bag with holes in it. He wasn't talking to lazy people.
He was talking to people who were busy, and tired, and couldn't figure out why it never felt like enough.

teach.h: DATED TO THE DAY: A TEMPLE IN RUINS.
teach.b: Haggai's first message is dated to the day: the second year of King Darius, the sixth month, the first day. The exiles have come home from Babylon to Jerusalem, and the temple is still a ruin.
People say it isn't the right time to rebuild. Haggai's answer, in the King James Bible: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

teach.h: PANELED HOUSES, A HOUSE IN RUBBLE.
teach.b: Cieled means paneled, finished nicely, while God's house sits in rubble. Then: "Consider your ways."

teach.h: SET YOUR HEART ON YOUR WAYS.
teach.b: In Hebrew it's more vivid: set your heart on your ways. Look hard at where your life is going.

Then the list: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes."
Every line has the same shape: effort in, nothing to show for it. Haggai's diagnosis is that the people have put their own houses first and left the center empty.
So the cure is surprisingly practical: go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build. Christians read Haggai more than one way. Some hear it about church buildings and giving.

Others hear it more broadly: when the most important thing in a life is left in ruins, everything else leaks. And the people listened. Before the month was out, by Haggai's own dates, they started rebuilding.

how: Some churches read Haggai when they are building or rebuilding, and some Christians use its call to consider your ways as a prompt for an honest review of how they spend their time and money.

o: set on a hill, high above the town
sealed shut, closed up and left empty
paneled, finished nicely, like a fine house

games.q: what's inside Haggai 1 — tap the pairs.

s: Haggai was talking to lazy people
they had sown much and worked hard. their effort leaked because the center was left in ruins.
Haggai's messages come with exact dates
his first message is dated to the day, in the second year of King Darius.
by his own dates, they started rebuilding before the month was out.

games.q: you're back from exile. your own house has nice paneling; the temple is rubble. people say it's not the right time. what does Haggai tell you to do?
o: consider your ways, then go and build.
games.why: "consider your ways," then go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build. and before the month was out, the people began.

practice: Picture your last week as a bag you've been filling with time, energy, money and attention, and find one hole: hours on a screen that left you emptier, or worry about something you can't change.
Then ask Haggai's question: what's the thing at the center I've left in ruins? If you pray, set it before God and ask for one first step; if not, simply name it, and name the first piece of wood.

wordCard.voice: Cieled. The old word for paneled, finished nicely: the houses Haggai says the people built for themselves while God's house lay in ruins.

orig.note: Hebrew: way, road, path. Haggai asks the people to set their hearts on their ways.

carryVoice: Your line: a bag with holes. The people listened, and started to build. Day four hundred ninety-three, done.
